summary.text: 次 is used for “next,” “in sequence,” and “second in rank.” Its early construction is disputed: interpretations include a military-station sign and human figures. Qin- and Han-period manuscripts attest ordered and ranked uses.

formation.text: The early construction is disputed. One analysis reads an oracle-bone graph as an early form of 師 with strokes indicating a military station. Other accounts interpret a human figure exhaling or speaking. Shuowen later analyzes 次 as 欠 plus 二 and assigns 二 a sound role; that account does not settle the earlier graph.

components.text: In Shuowen’s analysis, 欠 depicts an open-mouthed or exhaling person. Other interpretations also see a human figure, but do not establish 欠 as part of the earliest graph.
Shuowen assigns 二 a phonetic role in 次. Historical and modern reading comparisons can be reported, but do not establish that 二 supplied the sound.

sound_limitation.text: The modern Mandarin readings and Baxter–Sagart comparison do not independently establish 二 as 次’s phonetic component; the role remains disputed.

sound.text: In the Baxter–Sagart 2014 reconstruction, 二 and 次 share final material but differ in initial material. This comparison is relevant to the phonetic proposal, but does not establish 二’s role in 次.
The supplied local Mandarin readings are 二 èr and 次 cì. This current comparison does not establish a historical sound relationship.

history.text: Oracle-bone and bronze examples are recorded, followed by Qin-slip, seal, clerical, and regular-script forms. One interpretation connects an oracle-bone graph with an early form of 師 and reads it as a military-station sign; other accounts differ. This is a proposed graphic interpretation, not an established component breakdown.

Some bronze forms are described as having marks below 欠 or short strokes, but their significance is unresolved. Shuowen later analyzed 次 as 欠 plus 二 and assigned 二 a sound role; this historical analysis remains disputed.

uncertainties.text: Interpretations of the early graph differ: proposals include a military-station sign, an exhaling person, and a speaking figure with possible saliva marks. The available descriptions do not settle the construction.
Shuowen’s assignment of a sound role to 二 is historically important, but the reported modern and reconstructed reading comparisons do not independently confirm it.

No securely dated semantic path connects a proposed early meaning to “next” or “in sequence.” The lodging and tent examples come from transmitted texts whose witnesses are not dated in the cited accounts.

senses.gloss: in sequence; next or second in rank
senses.text: Qin- and Han-period manuscript citations attest 次 for ordered transmission and successive rank. These uses are established by that period, but do not show that they were the graph’s original meaning.
Transmitted texts use 次 for lodging or tents. How these uses relate to ranked and ordered meanings is unresolved.

A Han silk manuscript is reported to use 次 to write 恣. This is another word represented by the graph, not a demonstrated development in 次’s meaning. The account proposes sound-based borrowing, but supplies no pronunciations to compare; the proposed sound match therefore remains unverified here.

A Mawangdui manuscript is reported to use 次 where the transmitted Zhouyi has 濟. This is another word represented by the graph, not a demonstrated change in 次’s meaning. The account proposes sound-based borrowing, but supplies no pronunciations to compare; the proposed sound match therefore remains unverified here.

limitations.text: The Qin- and Han-period examples do not establish the first occurrence of ordered or ranked uses, or their derivation from any proposed original sense. No semantic link is asserted where the evidence does not demonstrate one.

次 is reported in place of 恣 and 濟 in separate manuscripts. The cited material gives no pronunciations to compare, so the proposed sound-based borrowing mechanism cannot be confirmed from this evidence.

overview.text: 次 means “next” or “in sequence.” Its early graph is read either as a military-station sign or as a human figure; the construction remains disputed. Qin- and Han-period manuscripts attest ordered and ranked uses.

components.text: In Shuowen’s analysis, 欠 pictures an open-mouthed or exhaling person; this does not settle the earliest graph’s form.
Shuowen treats 二 as a sound element, but the reported reading comparisons do not prove that it supplied 次’s sound.

relationships.text: In Shuowen’s analysis, 欠 pictorially represents an open-mouthed or exhaling person within 次.
Shuowen analyzes 二 as the phonetic element in 次; this role remains disputed.
